learningObjectives: Explain the physiological or methodological basis of Posterior Dominant Rhythm.
Apply Posterior Dominant Rhythm to technically valid clinical interpretation.
Identify artifacts, confounds and limits that could alter conclusions.
Communicate findings without exceeding the evidence or professional scope.

mechanismMap.label: Core concept
mechanismMap.detail: The posterior dominant rhythm is best seen over posterior regions with eyes closed and attenuates with eye opening or attention.

mechanismMap.label: Mechanism
mechanismMap.detail: Frequency changes with development and can slow with drowsiness, medication or diffuse cerebral dysfunction.

mechanismMap.label: Clinical integration
mechanismMap.detail: PDR frequency and reactivity help assess vigilance and diffuse dysfunction.

mechanismMap.label: Boundary condition
mechanismMap.detail: Calling all posterior alpha “relaxation” ignores age, task and pathology.

quizBank.question: Which statement best captures Posterior Dominant Rhythm?
options: The posterior dominant rhythm is best seen over posterior regions with eyes closed and attenuates with eye opening or attention.
It provides a stand-alone psychiatric diagnosis
It is unaffected by state and artifact
Its interpretation requires no clinical context
quizBank.explanation: The posterior dominant rhythm is best seen over posterior regions with eyes closed and attenuates with eye opening or attention.

quizBank.question: What is the safest clinical principle for Posterior Dominant Rhythm?
options: Integrate raw signal quality, state, method and clinical context
Assume a coloured map shows exact anatomy
Treat statistical rarity as proof of disorder
quizBank.explanation: EEG and QEEG interpretation requires converging evidence, technical validity and clinical context.

quizBank.question: Which error is most important to avoid in Posterior Dominant Rhythm?
options: Calling all posterior alpha “relaxation” ignores age, task and pathology.
quizBank.explanation: Calling all posterior alpha “relaxation” ignores age, task and pathology.

reviewPrompts.answer: Frequency changes with development and can slow with drowsiness, medication or diffuse cerebral dysfunction.
PDR frequency and reactivity help assess vigilance and diffuse dysfunction.
Calling all posterior alpha “relaxation” ignores age, task and pathology.
A rhythm is clinically meaningful only with location, state and reactivity.
